late-041.title: The last Denisovans
late-041.text: The Denisovans fade from view slowly. In their namesake cave in the Altai, the Denisova 3 finger bone dates to 76,200 to 51,600 years ago. They are confirmed there only until about 55,000 years ago. Elsewhere, Denisovan mitochondrial DNA in the sediments of the cave that held the Xiahe jaw spans 100,000 to 60,000 years ago, perhaps later. A Denisovan rib fragment from Baishiya Cave, China, is younger still, at 48,000 to 32,000 years ago.

late-072.title: Ice bulldozes the Dogger Bank
late-072.text: Dogger Bank began as mud on the bed of a glacial lake. Then the ice advanced and shoved those sediments into a ridge, a thrust moraine. This happened about 31,600 to 23,100 years ago.

late-073.title: Cave hyenas die out across Eurasia
late-073.text: Cave hyenas were apex predators that hunted horses, bison and aurochs. They ranged from Western Europe to Southeast Asia, and their bones are common in Last Glacial cave deposits. Their youngest well-dated European remains are about 31,000 years old, perhaps 24,000. In northeast Asia they lasted until about 20,000 years ago. Why they vanished is not fully understood. Climate alone seems insufficient, and human activity and dwindling prey probably contributed.

late-075.title: The Ito eruption forms the Aira Caldera
late-075.text: About 30,000 years ago, the colossal Ito eruption tore open Aira Caldera on Kyushu, spreading tephra and ignimbrite over the land. Seawater later flooded the caldera, helping form Kagoshima Bay, 200 m deep. Sakurajima volcano now rises inside it.

late-077.title: The Sahara dries as the Mousterian Pluvial ends
late-077.text: Until about 30,000 years ago, a long wet spell called the Mousterian Pluvial kept northern Africa well watered and cooler than today. When the pluvial ended, the Sahara turned arid. In the north of the Chad Basin, eolianite, sand dunes later hardened into rock, began to form 40,000 to 20,000 years ago.

late-076.title: Lake Bonneville begins to rise
late-076.text: About 30,000 years ago, a lake in Utah no bigger than today's Great Salt Lake began to grow. The name Lake Bonneville covers it from 30,000 to 13,000 years ago, while glaciers worldwide were expanded. It was not itself fed by an ice sheet's edge. After about 24,000 years ago it rose rapidly. It reached its highest level, the Bonneville shoreline, about 17,500 years ago.

late-079.title: Europe's ice-age megafauna at their peak
late-079.text: The cold was good for big animals, up to a point. Megafauna were most abundant in Europe around 27,000 to 21,000 years ago, thanks to the cold stadial climate. A mammoth steppe stretched from Spain across Eurasia and Beringia into Alaska and the Yukon. But as cold peaked in the Last Glacial Maximum, around 23,000 years ago, Europe's top predators began to die out.

late-080.title: The Last Glacial Maximum
late-080.text: Around 21,000 years ago, the world was about 6 °C colder on average than today. That may sound modest, but it buried continents. Ice sheets began advancing about 33,000 years ago in both hemispheres. Between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago they reached their greatest extent of the Last Glacial Period. This peak is the Last Glacial Maximum. Ice up to 3 km thick covered much of northern Europe, Asia and North America, as well as Greenland and Antarctica. In the Northern Hemisphere, people and animals retreated to refugia. These were sheltered areas where they could survive until the ice withdrew. The maximum also marks a turning point. From here the ice would begin to retreat, as told in {{ref:late-096}}.

late-081.title: Oruanui, the world's most recent supereruption
late-081.text: About 25,700 years ago, Taupō Volcano in New Zealand produced the most recent supereruption on Earth, rated VEI 8. It burst up through a system of lakes. Water and magma met, making it the largest phreatomagmatic eruption known, a blast driven by flashing steam. It produced about 530 km³ of magma as ash fall, ignimbrite and fill inside the caldera. Lake Huka was destroyed, and the caldera left behind now holds Lake Taupō. The eruption may have deepened the glacial cold in New Zealand and the nearby Pacific. Afterward the new lake filled to about 75 m above today's level, then cut through its ignimbrite dam less than 22,500 years ago.

late-082.title: Andean and Patagonian glaciers reach their peak
late-082.text: In the far south, the ice peaked a little earlier than in the north. Southern Hemisphere ice sheets grew from about 33,000 years ago. Northern Andean glaciers peaked around 27,000 years ago, and those of Chiloé 26,000 years ago, building a long moraine system. Around the Strait of Magellan, glaciers peaked 25,200 to 23,100 years ago. The Patagonian Ice Sheet covered all of Chile south of Puerto Montt and spilled into Argentina, where the dry climate stopped it.

late-083.title: The Laurentide ice sheet at its maximum
late-083.text: Ice once stood over Manhattan. After retreating between 52,000 and 40,000 years ago, the Laurentide Ice Sheet grew fast again. By the Late Wisconsin, about 25,000 to 21,000 years ago, North America's ice reached its maximum. It covered Canada east of the Rockies and pushed south to the Missouri and Ohio rivers. Ice sheets reached to about the 45th parallel north. In the Rockies, the Pinedale glaciation peaked 23,500 to 21,000 years ago.

late-084.title: Lake Sajsi on the Altiplano
late-084.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, a lake called Sajsi filled the Uyuni basin on the Bolivian Altiplano. It lasted from 25,000 to 19,000 years ago and was deepest 23,000 years ago. It was a forerunner of the larger Lake Tauca that would follow.

late-085.title: The Mal'ta boy and the Ancient North Eurasians
late-085.text: About 24,000 years ago, a boy was buried at Mal'ta, near Lake Baikal in Siberia, with artifacts and a Venus figurine. Mal'ta is the oldest known site in eastern Siberia. It had houses walled with bone and about thirty female figurines, a type previously found only in Europe. The boy's people, the Ancient North Eurasians, passed their genes to Native Americans, Siberians and Europeans alike.

late-086.title: The cave bear dies out
late-086.text: The cave bear of Europe and Asia died out about 24,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum. Its decline began long before. Ancient DNA shows its numbers falling steeply from about 40,000 years ago, as the Aurignacian began and modern humans arrived. By around 35,000 years ago it was no longer abundant in Central Europe.

late-088.title: Wild cereals harvested at Ohalo II
late-088.text: Long before farming, people were gathering grain. About 23,000 years ago, people near the Sea of Galilee were cultivating emmer, barley and oats. At Ohalo II, a lakeshore camp of that age, flint blades carry a gloss from cutting stems. They are the earliest known composite harvesting tools, blades set into handles. Humans were processing and eating wild cereal grains by then.

late-087.title: The White Sands footprints
late-087.text: In New Mexico's White Sands, people once walked across wet mud among ice-age animals. The site holds perhaps hundreds of thousands of human and animal tracks. Seeds in the layers date the human footprints to 23,000 to 21,000 years ago, during the Last Glacial Maximum. If correct, they are possibly the oldest evidence of people in the Americas. Skeptics say the seeds took up old carbon from groundwater. That would put the maximum age at only 15,500 to 13,500 years. Pollen and quartz-grain dating in 2023, and mud dating in 2025, supported the older ages. The debate continues.

late-089.title: The Fennoscandian ice sheet at its maximum
late-089.text: The ice of Scandinavia swallowed the mountains whole. The Fennoscandian Ice Sheet buried the entire Scandinavian Mountains. It reached the edge of the mid-Norwegian shelf by about 26,000 years ago, then merged with Barents Sea and British ice. It spread into Denmark, Germany, Poland and the former USSR. Its maximum came at different times in different places. It reached Denmark, Germany and western Poland about 22,000 years ago, and Lithuania and Belarus about 19,000. Its margin began to retreat 22,000 to 17,000 years ago.

late-090.title: The paintings of Lascaux
late-090.text: Lascaux Cave in France's Vézère valley holds some of the most celebrated paintings of the Upper Paleolithic. They show mainly large animals, matching the local wildlife known from fossils of the time. Many generations worked on them. Their age is still debated. The usual estimate, 17,000 to 22,000 years ago, places them in the early Magdalenian.

late-091.title: The Solutrean toolmakers of glacial Europe
late-091.text: During the Last Glacial Maximum, about 22,000 to 17,000 years ago, the Solutrean flint industry flourished in France, Spain and Portugal. It followed the Gravettian. Its people lived west of the Alps in a glacial refuge, between forest steppe and steppe tundra. They used toolmaking techniques not seen before and not rediscovered for millennia. Blended with earlier traditions, the Solutrean gave rise to the Magdalenian.

late-092.title: Sea level bottoms out at 125 m below today
late-092.text: Around 21,000 years ago, so much water was locked in ice, mostly in the Laurentide sheet, that the oceans stood about 125 m lower than today. Land bridges opened. The Bering land bridge joined Siberia and Alaska, and the Bassian Plain linked Tasmania to Australia. On the Great Barrier Reef, coral growth moved seaward with the falling water. It reached farthest from today's coast around 20,700 to 20,500 years ago.

late-093.title: Xianren Cave: the oldest pottery
late-093.text: Pottery was invented by hunters, not farmers. Sherds from Xianren Cave in Jiangxi, China, radiocarbon-dated to 20,000 to 19,000 years ago, are the earliest pottery known anywhere. Mobile foragers made the pots during the Last Glacial Maximum. Scorch marks suggest they cooked with them. Pottery had been thought to begin with the Neolithic, around 10,000 years ago.

late-096.title: The last deglaciation begins
late-096.text: Antarctica felt the thaw first. Around 22,000 years ago it warmed abruptly, by about 6 °C. The ice sheets had been largest between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. Northern warming began near 20,000 years ago, and northern ice began to retreat around 19,000 years ago. The start may have been sudden. A brief event, lasting at most 500 years, may have raised sea level by as much as 10 m, a surge called meltwater pulse 19ka. Northern warming stayed limited until about 14,600 years ago, and the retreat sped up around 15,000 years ago. The melting was neither steady nor simultaneous. Ice still covered most of Great Britain until about 16,000 years ago. The totals were vast. Over the whole deglaciation, global mean temperature rose about 5 °C and high latitudes over 10 °C. Sea level climbed more than 120 m.

late-095.title: The Southern Ocean breathes out carbon dioxide
late-095.text: Where did the carbon go during the ice age, and how did it come back? Ice cores show carbon dioxide at 180 to 210 ppm during ice ages, rising to 280 to 300 ppm in warm interglacials. During the Last Glacial Maximum, the extra carbon was stored in the deep ocean, held down by layering in the Southern Ocean. Over the deglaciation, about 19,000 to 11,000 years ago, stronger winds and retreating sea ice may have stirred the deep Southern Ocean and released it. The rise came in three abrupt pulses. It paused during the Antarctic Cold Reversal, 14,700 to 13,000 years ago. Rising carbon dioxide warmed the globe out of the glacial maximum. Its rapid increase eased about 11,500 years ago, as the deglaciation ended.

late-097.title: The Basal Pumice eruption and Vesuvius's Somma caldera
late-097.text: Vesuvius began forming about 25,000 years ago in the Codola eruption. From about 19,000 years ago it switched to large explosive, caldera-forming Plinian eruptions. About 18,300 years ago, the VEI 6 Basal Pumice eruption first formed the Somma caldera. Quieter lava eruptions followed. The most recent of its great Plinian blasts came in AD 79.

late-099.title: Rising seas begin to drown Sundaland
late-099.text: At the Last Glacial Maximum, with sea level about 120 m lower, Borneo, Java and Sumatra were joined to Asia. The whole Sunda Shelf lay exposed as dry land, called Sundaland. Around 18,000 years ago rising seas began to swallow part of it. The flooding went on until about 5000 BC.

late-098.title: The Oldest Dryas and Heinrich event 1
late-098.text: Just as the ice began to melt, the north plunged back into cold. The Oldest Dryas, a cold stadial, interrupted the retreat from about 18,000 to 14,700 years ago. Heinrich event 1 cooled the North Atlantic and weakened the ocean's overturning circulation. Rain belts shifted south, drying northern Africa. Europe was dry, treeless, grassy tundra. Iberian mountain glaciers that had nearly vanished surged back into the valleys 16,800 to 16,500 years ago. Yet species were already returning from refuges in the Carpathians, Italy, Spain and Greece, brown bears among them. Globally, rising carbon dioxide still warmed the planet about 2 °C, nearly half of it in the stadial's last centuries.

late-100.title: The Southern Hemisphere thaws fast
late-100.text: In southern Chile, rapid warming from 17,800 years ago brought interglacial temperatures within about 1,000 years. Glaciers retreated and Valdivian rainforest spread. A 2017 study linked a thinning of stratospheric ozone about 17,700 years ago to this sudden speed-up. The Patagonian Ice Sheet had peaked about 18,000 to 17,500 years ago, covering about 480,000 km² with over 500,000 km³ of ice. Its northern edge then melted rapidly. The meltwater freshened the nearby ocean and altered its circulation, with effects near and far. Around 18,000 years ago, glaciers also began to retreat on Antarctica's Alexander Island and melted from New Zealand's Tongariro.

late-101.title: Lake Tauca and the Central Andean Pluvial
late-101.text: On the Bolivian Altiplano, Lake Tauca rose from about 18,000 years ago. It peaked 16,500 years ago and stayed high until 15,500 years ago. The wetter first stage of the Central Andean Pluvial Event lasted from 17,500 to 15,900 years ago. Many explanations link the wet phase to circulation changes during Heinrich event 1, which carried more moisture onto the Altiplano.

late-102.title: The earliest true domestic dogs
late-102.text: The dog was the only animal people domesticated in the Pleistocene. The most widely accepted earliest dog is the Erralla dog from the Basque Country, Spain, dated 17,410 to 17,096 years ago. Disputed remains go back 36,000 years. The Bonn–Oberkassel dog, about 14,500 years old, is the oldest known dog buried together with people. People also brought dogs with them into North America.

late-103.title: The Bonneville flood
late-103.text: Lake Bonneville once covered about 83,000 km² of northern Utah. About 17,400 years ago it reached its highest level. Then it broke through a natural dam of alluvial fans at Red Rock Pass. A flood crest 120 m high raced toward the Snake River. At its peak, about 930,000 m³ of water passed every second. The torrent scoured the Snake River Canyon and created Shoshone Falls. It drained about 5,000 km³ of water and lowered the lake 107 m, to the Provo shoreline. Unlike the repeated Missoula floods, the Bonneville flood happened only once.

late-104.title: The Pacific coast opens a path south
late-104.text: Retreating glaciers on the Alaska Peninsula opened a way from Beringia to the Pacific coast by around 17,000 years ago. After that, the coastal corridor became livable. The ice barrier between interior Alaska and the coast broke up from about 16,200 years ago. The coast range was fully free of ice by 16,000 to 15,000 years ago. Kelp forests, estuaries and other shoreline habitats could have formed an open migration route.

late-105.title: A proposed Caspian flood into the Black Sea
late-105.text: Andrei Chepalyga proposed a flood from the Caspian into the Black Sea about 17,000 to 14,000 years ago. In his scenario, melting Scandinavian ice raised the Caspian up to 50 m above today's level from about 16,000 years ago. The water spilled west through the Manych–Kerch spillway. It would have raised the Black Sea by 60 to 70 m, flooding land once used for settlement or hunting. This 'Late Pleistocene Great Flood' is one researcher's hypothesis, not an established event.

late-106.title: The Vashon ice reaches Puget Sound
late-106.text: Ice once rolled over the site of Seattle. The Puget Lobe of the Cordilleran ice sheet passed there about 17,950 years ago and reached its maximum near Tenino about 16,950 years ago. From about 16,850 years ago it retreated about 340 m a year. A breached ice dam released a major outburst flood. By about 16,000 years ago, the ice had pulled back far enough for seawater to refill Puget Sound.

late-107.title: Woolly mammoths and rhinos retreat to the far north
late-107.text: As the ice age waned, the giants of the cold lost their ground. Woolly rhinos vanished from Europe 17,000 to 15,000 years ago. Their youngest reliable bones, from the Urals and northeast Siberia, are about 14,200 to 14,000 years old. Bølling–Allerød warmth likely brought more rain and snow, turning their low grass and herb habitat into shrubs and woods. Woolly mammoths disappeared from most of Europe by 14,000 years ago. They left Alaska and the Yukon about 13,300 years ago, roughly 1,000 years after people arrived. From about 15,000 years ago, wet tundra and forest replaced most of Siberia's mammoth steppe. By the Younger Dryas, mammoths survived only in its far north. DNA shows a final crash about 12,000 years ago, from which they never recovered. Whether habitat loss or hunting mattered more is still debated.

late-109.title: People spread through the Americas
late-109.text: Scholars agree on the basic story: the first Americans came from Siberia. They spread widely after the Last Glacial Maximum, around 16,000 to 13,000 years ago. Ice sheets blocked the inland routes until about 16,000 years ago. A route along the Pacific coast may have opened by 17,000 years ago. Around 16,000 years ago, the northern and southern Native American genetic branches split. Sites older than the Clovis culture, now widely accepted, trace the spread. Cooper's Ferry in Idaho dates to about 15,800 years ago. Page-Ladson in Florida dates to about 14,550, and Paisley Caves in Oregon to about 14,200. People reached South America around 15,000 years ago, before its megafauna died out.

late-108.title: The Baltic Ice Lake
late-108.text: Before the Baltic was a sea, it was a lake of meltwater. About 16,000 years ago, the retreating Weichselian ice reached the southern Baltic shore, and meltwater pooled along it. A well-defined Baltic Ice Lake existed by 14,600 years ago. By 13,000 BC it stretched from southern Sweden to Estonia. It lasted until about 11,700 years ago, close to the start of the Holocene.

late-110.title: Meadowcroft Rockshelter and the pre-Clovis debate
late-110.text: Radiocarbon dates suggest people used Meadowcroft Rockshelter in Pennsylvania from 16,000 years ago, possibly 19,000. That would put them there before the Clovis era. Critics suspect contamination by ancient carbon from local coal-bearing rock, though later tests support the early dates. Opinion stays split. A 2013 survey found that 38% of archaeologists accepted the dates and 20% rejected them.
